props.title: Meshes of the Afternoon

sections.content: Meshes of the Afternoon revolutionized experimental cinema through Maya Deren's hypnotic exploration of female psychological space. The film's circular narrative, where a woman (played by Deren) encounters multiple versions of herself in a dreamlike state, established core surrealist techniques that influenced directors like David Lynch and Darren Aronofsky. Its use of repetitive imagery - a key, a knife, a flower, a cloaked figure with a mirror for a face - created a visual language that would echo through Mulholland Drive (2001) and Black Swan (2010).

sections.content: The film's technical innovations remain striking today. Shot on 16mm with no dialogue, Deren and cinematographer Alexander Hammid created disorienting effects through creative camera angles, jump cuts, and slow motion. These techniques would influence the French New Wave, particularly Hiroshima Mon Amour (1959) and Last Year at Marienbad (1961), where reality and memory blur. The film's exploration of feminine domestic space as threatening and uncanny laid groundwork for psychological horror, evident in Repulsion (1965) and Rosemary's Baby (1968).

The repeated motifs and circular structure of Meshes of the Afternoon established a template for depicting fractured consciousness that resonates through modern cinema. Its influence appears in Persona (1966), where identity dissolves between two women, and 3 Women (1977), Robert Altman's dream-inspired character study. Contemporary filmmakers continue drawing from Deren's well - Mother! (2017) and The Lighthouse (2019) echo her surrealist approach to psychological deterioration. SUBHEAD: Legacy in Contemporary Cinema

Deren's innovative use of the female gaze and body in space continues influencing modern experimental and mainstream films. Under the Skin (2013) shares her abstract approach to female identity, while Horse Girl (2020) directly references her techniques in depicting mental disturbance. The film's DNA appears in music videos, particularly those directed by Chris Cunningham and Floria Sigismondi, who adopt its dreamlike repetitions and uncanny doubles.
